boil.description: Heat / boil (command 0x15 = 21). Arguments are the target temperature as one byte in degrees C (0x00-0x64 = 0-100) and the keep-warm time in minutes (0x00 off, 0x05-0x1e); iBrew's example `15 32 00 7e` heats to 50 C with no keep-warm. The legacy app's use of the second byte reads as a units flag instead, so treat it as keep-warm per iBrew and send 00.

device_info.description: Query device type + firmware (command 0x64 = 100). Reply `65 <type> <firmware> 7e` (0x65 = 101). The same frame is the UDP discovery broadcast.

enter_firmware_update.advanced_reason: Takes the kettle off your Wi-Fi and into its update access point, where it waits for a firmware image. Smarter's update service is gone, so there is no image to give it. The community notes get it back with a hard reset (hold the power button about ten seconds) or by pulling power for a moment; neither is verified here.
enter_firmware_update.description: Enter firmware-update mode (command 0x6d = 109). The kettle drops off the home Wi-Fi and raises its own "iKettle Update" access point; iBrew notes it also opens TCP port 6000 there.

reset_wifi.advanced_reason: Forgets the home Wi-Fi: the kettle drops off the network and has to be set up again from its access point.
reset_wifi.description: Join wireless network (command 0x0c = 12) with no SSID/password sent first: iBrew and ian-kent/ikettle2 both report that this resets the Wi-Fi to factory settings. The app's normal join sends `0c 7e 00 00 00 00 00 00` after the name and password frames.

methods.notes: Real discovery: broadcast the device-info frame `64 7e` (0x64 = 100) on UDP 2081; devices answer 0x65 (101) with their type + firmware. Broadcast may be dropped by the router — prefer a direct TCP connection.

device.name: Smarter iKettle 2.0 (and Smarter Coffee)
device.notes:
The Smarter iKettle 2.0 (and the same-protocol Smarter Coffee) are Wi-Fi kettles/coffee makers. Smarter is still a company, but the smart features for these devices were removed from the app in mid-2025 — owners report the kettles can no longer connect to the app, leaving "very expensive ordinary kettles". The LAN protocol needs no cloud at all, so it is the rescue path.
TRANSPORT: a binary protocol on port 2081, over UDP or TCP, no authentication. Message syntax: <id> <args> <terminator>, terminator always byte 0x7e ('~').
IDs are written as hex wire byte with decimal in brackets, "0x15 (21)". ian-kent/ikettle2 lists them in decimal, iBrew in bare hex, so the same command reads "21" in one and "15" in the other. A bare "21" or "22" put on the wire is a different command (iBrew lists 0x21 as heat-to-stored- defaults and 0x22 as an unknown kettle command), so the base matters. COMMANDS:
  0x15 (21)   heat / boil; args <temperature> <keep-warm minutes>
  0x16 (22)   stop heating
  0x64 (100)  get device info — also the UDP-broadcast discovery probe
  0x6d (109)  firmware-update mode (disables Wi-Fi, creates an "iKettle
              Update" AP)
RESPONSES:
  0x03 (3)    command status (ack)
  0x14 (20)   kettle status (flag byte, temperature, water level)
  0x65 (101)  device info reply, e.g. 65 01 13 7e = device type 0x01
              (kettle), firmware 0x13 (19)
Water-level quirk: the first level byte reads 7 with the kettle OFF its base, 8 when ON the base.
DISCOVERY: the device-info command 0x64 (100) is used over UDP broadcast after setup — but this fails on routers that do not forward UDP broadcasts, so a direct TCP connection to a known IP is the reliable path.
NOTE: the original iKettle (v1) uses an older, different protocol. This spec covers the 2.0 / Smarter Coffee family.

openness.notes: No vendor documentation. ian-kent/ikettle2 and iBrew reverse-engineered the protocol; iBrew tested against iKettle 2.0 firmware v19 and also drives Smarter Coffee.

credentials.notes: Onboarding passes the Wi-Fi credentials over the port-2081 protocol on the setup AP; no encryption is documented. Post-setup control is unauthenticated on the LAN.

factory_reset.description:
On the iKettle 2.0 the community-documented hard reset is holding the power button for about ten seconds; a client can also clear the Wi-Fi over the protocol (reset_wifi). Smarter's own reset article is for the 3rd generation, whose reset lives on the BASE with the kettle body lifted off. It is kept below as a variant procedure because it is the only vendor-documented one, not because it is known to work on a 2.0.
One detail that saves a support ticket (3rd generation, per Smarter): after the reset the connection light keeps flashing green, which looks exactly like the failure state it looked like before. That is normal, and it does not mean the reset did not take.
factory_reset.effect: Clears the stored WiFi credentials and the pairing, returning the base to onboarding so it can be given a new network.

procedures.basis: ian-kent/ikettle2 protocol notes: the recovery from command 0x6d (109)'s update mode is a hard reset holding the power button for 10 seconds.
procedures.name: Hold the power button for ten seconds (iKettle 2.0)

steps.action: Press and hold the kettle's power button for about ten seconds.
steps.expect: The kettle drops its network settings and comes back up in onboarding (not established which LED pattern confirms it).

procedures.basis: iBrew: command 0x0c (Join wireless network) sent without a preceding SSID/password resets the Wi-Fi to factory settings; ian-kent/ikettle2 says the same of command 12.
procedures.name: Clear Wi-Fi over the protocol (iKettle 2.0)

steps.action: Send reset_wifi on the port-2081 TCP session.
steps.expect: The kettle leaves the network and returns to its setup access point.

procedures.basis: Smarter's own support article on resetting the iKettle 3rd generation.
procedures.name: Base button held until three beeps, then a power cycle (3rd generation)

steps.action: Lift the kettle body off the base.
Press and hold the button on the base until it beeps three times.
Unplug the base for about ten seconds, then plug it back in.
steps.expect: The base is back in onboarding. A flashing green connection light at this point is normal.

methods.description: Join the kettle's setup AP and hand it the home Wi-Fi credentials over the port-2081 protocol; it reboots onto the LAN and answers device-info 0x64 (100) there.

steps.action: Power a new/reset kettle and join its setup AP.
Send the home Wi-Fi credentials over the port-2081 protocol.
steps.expect: The kettle joins the home network and answers the 0x64 (100) device-info probe.

setup.notes: A factory-fresh kettle hosts its own AP for Wi-Fi onboarding; joining it to the home network needs no cloud. The firmware-update command 0x6d (109) also creates an "iKettle Update" AP. Onboarding wire steps are not documented here.

rejoin.notes: No documented in-place Wi-Fi rewrite; treat a network change as a reprovision via the setup AP.

testing.notes: Not driven against hardware by this project. The port-2081 framing and command IDs are cross-checked between ian-kent/ikettle2 and iBrew (which tested against iKettle 2.0 firmware v19).

dfu_mode.notes: The kettle leaves the home network and hosts the "iKettle Update" access point instead; whether the SSID carries a suffix is not established. A client that loses the kettle on the LAN and sees this AP should report it as mid-update, not as a new device.

image.notes: The vendor's update service went with the rest of the smart features in 2025. No image source is known.

dfu.notes: Entry and the update AP are from the community protocol notes (ian-kent/ikettle2, iBrew), not hardware-verified. The legacy app's own update path (research-notes/smarter-ikettle.md, app-derived and not cross-checked) sends an update-init frame `6E 7E`, then `70 <len32> 7E` followed by 261-byte image blocks with a `7E 7E 7E` trailer, over the port-2081 TCP session. How that relates to command 0x6d (109) and the update AP (same flow, or two paths) is not established; neither ian-kent/ikettle2 nor iBrew lists 0x6e (110) or 0x70 (112), so the mechanism is `custom` and `6E` is not declared as a command.
